 Neighbors hope that LA thinks of unhoused residents during El Niño winter 
 Thursday’s storm gives LA a taste of a wet, El Niño winter that’s expected to linger for the next few months. 
 by 
 Nick Ducassi 
 Nov. 19, 2026 Nov. 19, 2026

 Unhoused residents are most at risk during rainy winter season in dense neighborhoods like Koreatown, according to volunteer outreach groups. (Nathan Solis/The LA Local) 
 A strong November rain drenched Los Angeles Thursday morning, leaving behind flooded streets and giving residents a taste of what El Niño has in store for the city. Some local groups hope the weather encourages residents to help their unhoused neighbors as the rain season is underway .
 Neighborhoods around downtown Los Angeles, including Koreatown, Pico Union and Westlake, received about an inch of rain between 5:30 a.m. and 11:30 a.m., according to the National Weather Service. That’s especially difficult for residents, commuters and the unhoused.
 Heavy rains present many challenges for people living on the streets, KTown For All volunteer Ayla Dvoretzky said.
 The advocacy group provides direct aid to people experiencing homelessness in Koreatown and volunteers have been helping unhoused community members prepare for heavy rains. The group is working with representatives from City Council District 1 to inform and educate the community.

 Residents along Wilshire Boulevard make their way through a November rain storm. Forecasts show that the wet, rainy conditions will persist with the El Niño conditions. (Nathan Solis/The LA Local) 
 Dvoretzky points out that people who live in areas with illegal dumping, such as alleyways, are especially at risk. 
 “The rain washes all that down … and that water also just ran through like trash or chemical waste or rat feces from the street, and so you end up with a really intense kind of like biohazard risk,” Dvoretzky said.
 While KTown for All does its best to distribute donations as they come in, Dvoretzky said much of the group’s work comes down to removing barriers between Koreatown residents and their unhoused neighbors. 
 “Getting over that fear of approaching … can help you make a lot of really direct impact,” she said. 
 As a Koreatown resident herself, she said it’s “extra meaningful to know and be able to recognize the person to whom your support is going. Removing the middleman, I think, is a really good way to just kind of change the culture of things overall.”
 Like other mutual aid groups, KTown For All distributes plastic bags to protect important documents, tents, tarps, duct tape, weather forecast printouts and warm, waterproof clothing. After they rain, the group also makes an effort to hand out quarters and detergent pods to help people wash their clothes.
 Representatives from Council District 1 have also offered to help inform unhoused residents about weather risks, according to Dvoretzky. Other forms of help is also available through the Koreatown Rapid Response Team  who can clear debris from neighborhood storm drains. 
 The storm barreled through Los Angeles and left a lot of rain behind. In the San Fernando Valley, some neighborhoods received over 2 inches of rain in a matter of an hour on Thursday, according to the National Weather Service.
 “We received a lot of rain in a short period of time that will continue to cause flooded roadways, downed trees, and potential mud and debris flows,” Mayor Karen Bass said in a news advisory on Thursday morning. The city encourages residents to sign up for emergency alerts at NotifyLA.org and report any flooding, fallen trees, or other damage that is non-life-threatening to 311.
 The rain is expected to pass through Los Angeles by Friday evening, leaving behind cooler temperatures over the weekend, Meteorologist Mike Wofford with the National Weather Service said.
 There’s a possibility for more rain Sunday evening and into Monday morning, but residents should get used to these types of unusually strong storm systems.
 “We have got abnormally warm ocean waters, somewhere in the 70 degrees, and that will contribute to extra moisture in the air,” Wofford said, referring to the El Niño conditions persisting for the next several months.
